html_body:
You Don't Need A PhD To Invest Like A Scientist

Kyle Grieve borrows nine mental models from physics, chemistry, and biology and turns them into tools for reading businesses.

Episode: Unlocking Hidden Investing Secrets From Basic Science — 30 August 2025

“Have you ever wondered if the secrets to smarter investing might be hidden in some overlooked scientific principles?” That is how Kyle Grieve opens this solo episode — and his answer is a confident yes. Physics, chemistry, and biology are not school subjects you have forgotten; they are a toolbox for spotting good businesses and dodging bad ones. The promise of the episode is that the same forces that move particles and organisms also move companies, and that naming them makes you a clearer thinker.

TL;DR

Grieve walks through nine mental models, drawn largely from Shane Parrish’s The Great Mental Models, Volume 2, plus a few personal favorites. The pitch is refreshingly unpretentious. Each model — relativity, inertia, momentum, leverage, catalysts, ecosystems, niche, signaling, and incentives — is a lens for asking a sharper question about a company than the spreadsheet alone will answer.

The Core Idea

The hard sciences have spent centuries naming forces that also quietly govern businesses and markets. Borrow the vocabulary, Grieve argues, and you get a faster way to reason about why one company compounds for decades while another stalls. He is explicit that biology is his favorite well to draw from — the messy, adaptive, incentive-driven science maps unusually well onto how companies actually behave.

The best part, you don’t need a PhD to use them. All you need is an understanding of what they are and how to apply them to solve problems. — Kyle Grieve

Crucially, the models are not a valuation formula. They are prompts. Relativity asks you to change your vantage point; inertia asks whether a business is coasting or genuinely improving. Used together, they form a checklist for the qualitative side of investing that the numbers tend to miss — the part of the analysis that decides whether a cheap stock is a bargain or a trap. That qualitative read is exactly where most spreadsheets go quiet, and where a good lens earns its keep.

The Nine Models, Decoded

The nine lenses Grieve promises to walk through, with the angle he frames for each:

  • Relativity — the same company looks different depending on where you stand; deliberately switching perspectives surfaces opportunities other investors miss.
  • Inertia — businesses, like objects, resist changing course. It reveals which companies stay great and which stay stuck, decade after decade.
  • Momentum — small advantages compound into flywheels; momentum in the fundamentals is often more telling than momentum in the share price.
  • Leverage — a force multiplier that cuts both ways, accelerating growth on the way up and dangerously magnifying risk on the way down.
  • Catalysts — the events that rapidly unlock a thesis, turning a slow-burning idea into a fast one.
  • Ecosystems — change one input and value multiplies across everything connected to it; strong ecosystems compound advantages.
  • Niche — narrow, specialized strategies can create outsized, defensible advantages that broad competitors cannot easily copy.
  • Honest vs. dishonest signals — borrowed from biology; learning to tell a costly, credible signal from cheap talk helps you cut through market noise.
  • Misaligned incentives — the quiet risk multiplier; when management’s incentives point away from shareholders’, trouble compounds unseen.

How To Actually Use This

The practical move is to run a company through the models as questions. Is this business coasting on inertia or building momentum? Is management sending honest signals or cheap ones? Are the incentives aligned, or is risk quietly accumulating? None of this requires a discounted-cash-flow model — it requires attention.

The lenses double as a bias check. If you only ever look at a company from one vantage point, you will keep missing what a shift in perspective — relativity — would reveal. The discipline is in cycling through all nine before you fall in love with a thesis: a business can pass the momentum test and still fail the incentives test, and it only takes one broken lens to sink an otherwise attractive idea. Treated as a pre-mortem rather than a sales pitch, the framework is most valuable when it talks you out of a position you already wanted to buy.

Where It Breaks Down

A fair caution the framing invites: analogies from science are lenses, not laws. A metaphor that fits too neatly can flatter a bad idea. Momentum reverses. Leverage that looked like an accelerant becomes an anchor when the cycle turns. A “moat” that looks like a defensible niche can turn out to be a small, shrinking market. The models earn their keep as questions that pressure-test an idea — and lose it the moment they become the reason you stop asking questions. The scientist’s real habit worth copying is not the metaphor; it is the willingness to look for evidence that you are wrong.

Books & resources mentioned:

  • The Great Mental Models, Volume 2: Physics, Chemistry and Biology — Shane Parrish
